sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text:
Áeb, also written Aebh or Aobh, is an Irish heroine. In the story of the Children of Lir, she is the birth mother of the fated children of the title. The Children of Lir is among the best known of Irish legends.

Áeb was the daughter of Bodb Derg, a great magician. She was the wife of Lir, and the children of the title were born to them. She died giving birth to her second set of twins. Her only daughter, Fionnuala, is the heroine of the tale. Fionnuala replaced her mother after the children were bereaved. She gave the orphaned children the care their mother could no longer offer.

Áeb's death brought her childless fostersister, Aífe, into Lir's household. Aífe was cruel. Her jealousy of the children grew until she laid a curse. The curse turned Áeb's children into singing swans. The children lived on in swan form for nine hundred years.

The account of Áeb is brief, but it sets the whole tragedy in motion. Her early death left the children without a protector. It opened the way for Aífe's malice to reach them. Fionnuala's loyalty becomes the counterweight to that cruelty. Through the long years of swan form, she stayed steadfast at their side.

The tale shows how a single loss can ripple through a family. Áeb's death is the pivot on which the whole story turns. Her memory endures in the loyalty of her daughter Fionnuala. The singing swans of the Children of Lir carry her name through Irish legend. She remains the quiet figure behind one of the great sorrows of Irish myth.
objective: To record who Áeb was and how her death set in motion the tragedy of the Children of Lir.
